business_flow: The captured traffic is from a web application with mixed public and authenticated endpoints. Observed endpoints include root (/), /admin, /login (GET/POST), /logout, /my-account (with id parameter), /role-selector (GET/POST), /resources, /image, and /academyLabHeader. Several requests include session cookies with different session values. A notable request is GET /my-account?id=wiener which returns 200 and appears to accept a user identifier in a query parameter. Other endpoints either returned non-200 statuses or have no body/evidence in the log.
thought_process: Examine each of the 15 entries and apply the five checks: IDOR (BLA9), State Manipulation (BLA3), Sequence Bypass (BLA6), Shadow Endpoints (BLA10), Internal Disclosure (BLA8).

Only create findings where evidence in the traffic indicates a likely business logic vulnerability. Do not invent vulnerabilities where the captured request/response does not show exploitable behavior.
Ensure one finding per endpoint when a vulnerability is present, with a PoC containing payload_mutation and a curl_command using placeholders.

potential_vulnerabilities.description: The /my-account endpoint accepts an 'id' query parameter (GET /my-account?id=wiener) and returned HTTP 200. This indicates the application may be using a direct object reference (username) passed as a client-controlled parameter to fetch account pages. If there is no server-side ownership/authorization check, an attacker could change the 'id' parameter to view other users' account pages (IDOR). The captured traffic shows an authenticated session cookie was present when requesting this endpoint, suggesting the endpoint discloses user-specific account information based on the id. This is consistent with Broken Access Control / IDOR (BLA9).

reproduction_guide.payload_mutation: Change the 'id' parameter from 'wiener' to another victim username or identifier (e.g., 'carlos' or '{{target_id}}') to attempt to view that user's account.
